title: Hello [Open] World: Unbody Is Now OSS (Alpha)
author: amir
blurb: Unbody, the AI-native backend, is now open source (Alpha), inviting developers to build transparent and trustworthy AI systems. Designed as the "Supabase of the AI era," it offers a modular architecture that transforms raw data into reasoning-ready knowledge.

summary.summary: Unbody introduces itself as the first modular backend for the AI-native era, built in the open.
It is a data-knowledge-driven, AI-native backend designed to replace traditional stacks.
The system is architected for modularity, autonomous agent support, and plugin extensibility.
Unbody aims to build the Supabase of the AI era and invites developers to help shape it.
The source code is available at github.com/unbody-io/unbody.
Launching Unbody commercially last year revealed that building an excellent product requires involving the wider developer community.
One truth became clear: building an excellent product requires involving the wider developer community.
Unbody is releasing as open source to build a better product and gain developer adoption.
We believe open source allows for the inspection and customization necessary to build transparent and trustworthy AI software.
This alpha release prioritizes architectural flexibility and modularity over feature completeness to allow easy extension.
The modular design supports traditional plugins and autonomous AI agents that process information.
The Contextual Data Engine transforms raw, fragmented data into structured, queryable, and interconnected knowledge.
The architecture is designed for integration with tools like Unstructured.io and LlamaIndex.
The open-source version already outclasses the cloud service in terms of architectural openness and modularity.
While the cloud offering has production-grade features, it comes with trade-offs like locked-in storage and inflexible pipelines.
The open-source version offers greater flexibility to choose storage solutions, AI models, and customize processing pipelines.
Despite significant refactors, the content API remains unchanged to let users interact with the knowledge base as usual.
The roadmap envisions eventually replacing the cloud version with this open-source powerhouse.
We are sharing Unbody OSS Alpha to open a discussion with the community and ensure we build something people want.
The AI tooling ecosystem is scattered and complex, often requiring developers to make dozens of stack decisions.
Unbody asks what if there were a Supabase, but specifically for the AI era.
Supabase simplified building modern web apps by handling databases, auth, and storage in a unified stack.
Unbody aims to bring that same spirit to AI-native software that reasons, adapts, and acts.
Supabase is great, but it wasn't built for a world where your backend needs to think.
Traditional stacks store static data, whereas AI-native products demand a different approach.
The way we interact with software has fundamentally changed.
We no longer just click buttons; we talk to software and expect it to reason and act.
Unlike passive legacy software, AI-native software is active, context-aware, and requires managing dynamic knowledge.
AI-native software needs enriched, connected knowledge rather than just rows in tables to enable reasoning.
To mimic human intelligence, software needs a dynamic graph of meaning rather than rigid schemas.
Essential infrastructure like ingestion, vectorization, and summarization is often left to be duct-taped together.
A backend that understands like a human must process text, images, video, and audio.
Unbody is a Supabase-style stack for building AI-native products from the ground up.
Without Unbody, even building a simple Q&A bot requires significant effort.
Building a bot usually requires spinning up a vector database like Weaviate or Pinecone.
Developers normally must create a pipeline for chunking and ingesting content.
All these components must be stitched into the backend and maintained.
Unbody offers opinionated flexibility, allowing you to bring your own vector store or AI provider without lock-in.
An image displays the Unbody modular stack architecture.
The GitHub repo README contains in-depth information and a complete list of modules and plugins.
Since software is becoming more like humans, the backend that powers it needs to work like a brain.
Unbody is built on four functional layers that mirror how intelligent systems operate.
The Perception layer handles Knowledge Fabrication and how the system sees the world.
The Memory layer handles storage and persistent memory regarding what the system knows.
The Reasoning layer governs AI and autonomy to determine how the system thinks.
The Action layer uses APIs and MCP to interact with others and take initiative.
This section defines where raw data becomes structured, enriched knowledge.
Data Ingestion connects and pulls content from third-party platforms, files, and databases.
Processing automatically parses and structures raw multi-modal data from various formats.
Enhancement transforms raw data into semantic knowledge using pluggable enhancer agents.
Vectorization generates semantic vector representations using models like OpenAI or Cohere.
This section covers where enriched knowledge lives and is ready for retrieval.
Vector Storage keeps embeddings in databases like Weaviate, Pinecone, or Qdrant.
File Storage persists raw and processed files using local storage, S3, or GCS.
Media Serving allows access to media through Unbody’s CDN and signed URLs.
Metadata Store keeps track of content structure, relationships, and context.
This section describes where intelligence, generation, and decision-making happen.
Text Generation includes built-in support for models like GPT-4 and Claude via hosted APIs or self-hosting.
JSON Generation produces structured responses and machine-readable payloads.
Image Generation is on the roadmap to provide cloud-only support for visual generation.
Function Registry defines callable functions for agents via schema-based definitions.
Execution & Routing dynamically executes functions with intent parsing and argument validation.
This section explains how the backend connects to the outside world.
Content API allows querying the knowledge-base via GraphQL with semantic capabilities.
Push API pushes structured data directly into Unbody.
Admin API configures schemas, projects, pipelines, and permissions.
Middleware Control Plane connects Unbody to external systems and workflows.
SDKs are available in TypeScript, iOS, and Android.
The API provides chat endpoints with memory and long-term context.
It supports integration with observability monitoring systems.
Unbody is currently in feedback mode to know what works and what needs improvement.
The alpha is released to build with community feedback, so please give Unbody Alpha a try.
Link to the Unbody GitHub Repo.

title: Managing the UI state for generative data flow
author: amir
blurb: Generative AI requires a fundamental shift in how we manage UI state, moving from atomic CRUD requests to multi-stage, streaming, and interpretative flows. This post outlines the conceptual foundation for building robust generative user interfaces.

summary.summary: While wiring up the UI for a basic agentic RAG layer, I realized the state model felt incompatible with normal fetch/response flows.
I realized the problem wasn’t the code, but the mental model, as we were still thinking like CRUD developers.
This post explains the conceptual foundation of what actually makes UI state management for generative flows different.
Before we talk about managing it, we need to define it.
Generative data is any output produced on the fly by a model, including text generation and RAG responses.
To keep the discussion grounded, we’ll use RAG as the main example, though the principles apply to any generative pattern.
To make this clearer, it helps to contrast it with something we do understand: the CRUD model.
This image compares generative data versus CRUD data.
RAG helps you combine a user’s question with relevant data from your own sources to generate a response.
This visual illustrates the RAG flow: retrieve, generate, and respond.
The first step is to retrieve relevant content from your data, such as documents or database records.
The second step is to generate an answer using that retrieved content as context.
This setup grounds generation in real, retrievable context rather than just what the model was trained on.
We’ll use this flow throughout the rest of the post as our working example.
In CRUD flows, the data is a fact, and it’s complete when it arrives.
In generative flows, the data is an interpretation that is built in real time and often streamed.
That distinction leads to three fundamental differences in how we need to think about state.
A CRUD request is typically atomic: one request, one response.
This image depicts the CRUD one-shot atomic request and response model.
In RAG and most gen workflows, the process is multi-step with at least two stages.
This graphic shows a minimal RAG multi-stage pipeline: retrieve then generate.
And that’s just the minimal case, as a more realistic setup might include additional steps.
This diagram displays a realistic multi-stage generative pipeline with additional steps.
Each of these stages can fail independently, so a single loading or error flag breaks immediately.
In gen flows, the payload streams in over time—often token by token—rather than arriving all at once.
Sometimes this streams sequentially, but other times it involves non-monotonic updates or image refinement.
If you're not thinking in terms of partial state and streaming updates, you'll either show nothing or constantly overwrite your UI.
This illustration contrasts parcel delivery with streaming token-by-token output.
Here’s a simplified example of how gen output is typically handled in practice.
You don’t get the data all at once; you build it as it arrives.
In CRUD flows, the data is a fact that is precise, repeatable, and complete.
This visual comparison highlights that CRUD returns facts while generative returns interpretations.
Generative responses are an interpretation shaped by input, context, and the model’s probabilistic behavior.
Even when grounded with the same input data, the output can vary slightly in tone or wording.
In generative systems, the response is a version of the truth, unlike the absolute truth in CRUD.
That distinction changes what you can assume about the output and how you treat it in your UI.
The way you manage state has to change once you understand that generative data is multi-stage, streamed, and interpretative.
Generative outputs aren’t returned all at once; for example, you get a readable stream of text tokens.
So instead of setting the final result, you append tokens as they arrive.
You also need to support canceling the stream immediately because tokens cost money and users might change their input.
This graphic demonstrates streaming with append and cancel support.
Without cancel support, you’ll burn tokens unnecessarily.
Without append logic, you can’t reflect progress in the UI.
Context is the real state you need to manage.
The composition of pipeline stages—retrieval, augmentation, generation—is what we call context.
You should treat the context as a first-class application state object, just like a Redux store.
Here’s an example of what a structured context might look like in a RAG system.
This diagram details a sample context structure for a RAG system.
The retrieved records, conversation history, and intermediate states are what made the output possible.
Discarding context essentially means throwing away the trace of your reasoning.
This is the actual state of your generative UI.
From a frontend perspective, your component should be bound to the context representing what the model saw.
When users regenerate or edit, this context is your truth, not the model’s output.
From a UI perspective, the context becomes a kinds of contract between the system and the user.
It implies that given this context, this is the best interpretation we could generate.
This makes it easier to justify or explain things if your users ask why it said that.
Once you understand that generation is a pipeline, the next shift is in how you model state in your UI.
In a gen flow, you have multiple steps, so you often cannot get away with a simple isLoading flag.
So your app needs to treat each stage as its own state machine.
Union types guarantee that you’re never in conflicting states, like being both loading and done.
You can give precise feedback to the user, transitioning from retrieving sources to generating an answer.
You can retry only part of the flow, such as retrying just generation if retrieval was fine.
Your UI logic becomes much easier to manage when you switch on state.
In generative flows, retries are a feature, not just a mechanism for network failures.
Sometimes the model fails to produce a valid output, or you just want a second version.
Because every stage is separate, retries should also be stage-aware.
This visual represents a stage-aware retry flow in generative pipelines.
Managing UI state for generative data involves keeping track of context and understanding the shape of your pipeline.
This applies to RAG, calling OpenAI functions, chaining LLM tools, or any UI built on generative outputs.
We’re considering a follow-up post focused purely on the engineering mechanics if you're curious about that side.
I’d love to hear from you if you're building generative features and thinking about developer ergonomics.

title: AI in 2023: Paradoxical Advancement
author: amir
blurb: Despite 2023 being a year of incredible advancements in AI, a stark contrast remains between these technological leaps and their limited real-world applications in business. This post explores the gap between passive data and actionable knowledge.

summary.summary: This text focuses on bridging the increasing gap between AI as tech and its applications.
While 2023 was marked by incredible advancements in AI, there is a stark contrast between these technological leaps and their real-world applications in the business sector.
The potential for AI to transform passive data into actionable knowledge remains largely untapped in practical business applications.
This section outlines examples of untapped AI potential in industries.
Specific industry scenarios highlight how AI's transformative potential remains largely untapped despite its capability to address critical business challenges.
In the legal sector, AI can automate case research and predict legal outcomes, yet this application is rarely seen in practice.
Adoption in the healthcare industry is sporadic and largely confined to experimental segments rather than widespread clinical practice.
The publishing industry continues to rely on traditional methods, with AI-driven innovations for content curation and layout design being more of an exception.
These examples underscore a significant gap where practical application effectively addressing industry-specific challenges is still in its nascent stages.
The complexity of AI technology often focuses on enhancing capabilities rather than practical applications, limiting its use in business.
Technologically sophisticated tools frequently necessitate specialized knowledge to operate, creating a barrier to widespread adoption in everyday business operations.
Input from creative minds and business strategists is crucial to transform AI from a niche technology into a user-friendly tool.
Unbody was created as a low-code privacy-friendly platform to democratize AI technology and simplify tools for a wider audience.
We are ready to look at ways to help law firms, websites, and publishing leverage visual search and AI-driven content management.
As we look towards the future, unlocking AI's full potential requires bridging the gap between technological capabilities and practical applications.

title: From Query to Context: Building Agentic RAG with Unbody's JSON Endpoint
author: amir
blurb: Learn how to upgrade from naive retrieval to Agentic RAG by parsing complex user queries into structured parameters. This guide demonstrates how to build a smart pipeline that understands potential constraints and filters using Unbody's JSON endpoint.

summary.summary: I recently spoke at AI Thinkers Abu Dhabi about how a naive approach to RAG often isn't enough.
Real user queries, like asking for an Italian dish ready in under 30 minutes, can be nuanced.
Agentic RAG improves results by parsing the query into structured parameters like "no sausage" or "under 30 minutes".
Let’s see how to do this with Unbody step by step.
You need an Unbody project set up with your data already ingested and indexed.
You need your API key and Project ID from the Unbody dashboard.
If you haven’t set this up yet, check out the Unbody docs for a quick start.
That’s it, now you can start calling Unbody’s APIs to search, filter, and generate.
Knowing the schema tells us exactly which parameters we can extract from a user’s query.
Knowing these fields lets us decide which parts of the user’s query should be parsed and parameterized.
For example, a user might request an Italian dish with no sausage ready in under 30 minutes.
We know to extract the concept, ingredients to exclude, and a time constraint from this query.
RAG consists of Retrieval and Generation, where retrieval gathers context for the model.
One approach is to take the user’s entire query text.
Then feed the top documents into a text-generation prompt.
This naive system doesn’t actually understand the user’s intention and fails with multiple constraints.
A better approach is to parse the user’s query into structured parameters.
Then appy filters to our knowledge base, such as "exclude sausage" or "max 30 minutes".
Finally, generate the final response using only the truly relevant documents.
The general syntax we will be using is with Unbody’s chain syntax methods.
To translate this into a proper RAG query, we need to extract three pieces of information.
First, we need main keywords or concepts to apply to semantic search.
Second, we need any specific filters to pass to the where function.
Third, we need the prompt or task description for the generation step.
We will use Unbody’s generative JSON endpoint which utilizes the Zod library to define output.
Unbody’s generative JSON receives two arguments: a set of messages and a Zod schema.
In the Zod schema, we differentiate the shape of the JSON, starting with the concepts field.
We are expecting an array of strings or null if no concepts are extracted.
The describe method adds a note explaining that this field represents the main search terms.
Next, we capture ingredients that the user wants to include in the same way.
The description clarifies that this field is for ingredients the user explicitly wants.
Example fields might include preferred cuisine types or time limits.
We can include preferred cuisine types in the schema.
We can also include a maximum time constraint in minutes.
Here is the full Zod schema with descriptions for every field.
We create a function called queryParser and integrate the logic into it.
We pass our complete querySchema to the generative endpoint.
The system message instructs the model to analyze the query.
The returned payload provides a well-structured object containing all extracted parameters.
The model processes the user’s input and returns a structured JSON object for precise queries.
Now that we’ve parsed the query, it’s time to build the final RAG pipeline.
We search based on extracted concepts, falling back to the full query if needed.
This ensures that our semantic search is as focused as possible.
We must turn each extracted filter into a proper "where" clause.
If the query has an includeIngredients array, we want to add a filter for it.
We use a conditional to add this filter only when includeIngredients exists.
We conditionally spread the filter or simply add an empty array if it doesn't exist.
If the query specifies ingredients to exclude, we add a filter for each item.
Each ingredient to exclude is mapped into a NotEqual filter conditionally.
We are combining all filters using the And operator.
Finally, we combine all these filters into a single query.
This combined filter only adds a condition if that parameter exists.
We proceed to generating the final answer with the fromMany method.
We use the generation step to produce a final, coherent answer after retrieval.
The system message instructs the model to consider the retrieved results when generating.
This brings it all together into the complete RAG pipeline.
Here is what the full API handler might look like in a Next.js project.
The query is processed by parseQuery to return formatted parameters like concepts and constraints.
The semantic search focuses specifically on the extracted concepts.
The filtering applies each filter conditionally using the And operator.
The autocut method limits our result set to a manageable size.
Finally, the generate method produces a coherent answer integrating the retrieved documents.
Check out the full demo of this Agentic RAG system in action on YouTube.
You can find the complete source code for this project on GitHub.
The source is available in the example Next.js repository under recipes.
With Unbody’s Agentic RAG approach, you capture intention and filter precisely.
Are you ready to build smarter, AI-native applications?
Experiment with the sample code and start tailoring your own Agentic RAG pipeline.
Check out the Unbody documentation for further insights and advanced use cases.
Share your projects, ideas, or questions on our community forums.
Consider joining our open-source community to help shape the future of intelligent applications.
Happy building, and let’s push the boundaries of what our applications can do together.

We will use Unbody to convert input video into intelligence and Appsmith to build the UI without extensive coding, offering a customized alternative to tools like Otter.ai.

title: What the F**k is an AI-native app?
author: amir
blurb: Discover why 'AI-first' is becoming the new 'mobile-first' and what it truly means to build AI-native applications. This post breaks down the three pillars of AI-native design—personalization, context, and conversational interaction—and explains how to implement them without reinventing the wheel.

summary.summary: AI-first is becoming the new mobile-first, prompting a dive into the characteristics of AI-native apps.
The prevalence of LLMs necessitates a shift in user mentality and software design similar to the 'mobile-first' mindset.
An AI-native app is defined as more human software that understands and adopts to the human user.
Software needs the ability to adapt and tailor to our individual needs and contexts, such as work versus home personas.
A chatbot app at work must understand your company, department, and team to effectively search documents.
We need software to access and understand the data footprints we produce daily to provide a personalized experience.
Traditionally, CMS platforms require considerable manual effort to create and manage structured data.
Image illustrating traditional versus AI-native data management approaches for personalization.
Much existing information, like FAQs or docs, traditionally requires re-curation to fit structured data requirements.
AI-native applications use AI to transformation data, allowing us to maintain it in its original format and location.
This process requires the capability to aggregate and process documents and data from all different locations.
A crucial aspect of AI-native apps is preserving the interconnected context of content rather than isolating it.
Image showing context awareness through semantically connected data sources.
Making connections between different 'islands' of information defines context, which is a critical element for AI-native applications.
We need semantically connected topics via features like 'semantic search' to provide contextually connected responses.
Users now expect to communicate with apps and websites through conversation, not just by clicking through options.
Image depicting the shift from information seeking to conversational interaction with software.
There is a growing preference for using natural human language when interacting with software.
To support interactive approaches, we need features like generative search, image captioning, and chatbots.
Image showing a technical breakdown of AI-native app components.
The essential tech for AI-first apps breaks down into three main areas: aggregation, processing, and functions.
Data Aggregation is about getting data from different places and making sure it all syncs up nicely.
Data Processing involves turning raw data into AI-ready data through cleaning, chunking, and vectorizing.
The third area covers functions, borrowing from RAG but going beyond specific technical definitions.
Data Retrieval acts as a supercharged search engine inside your app to find exactly what you need.
Data Augmentation is about making existing data better by adding new details or tweaking it for context.
Data Generation creates new bits of content on the spot based on what users are asking for.
Here is a peek at what it looks like to assemble a system that can handle everything discussed.
Image illustrating the complexity of assembling a full AI-native system from scratch.
Building this system generally requires Python knowledge and putting together about ten different components like LLMs and vector stores.
Beyond AI elements, real-world apps also utilize CDNs and media hosting to ensure performance.
Unbody is developing an AI-as-a-service platform that automates the entire AI development pipeline for developers.
Image demonstrating how Unbody simplifies AI-native app development.
Unbody automates the aggregation and processing of data from sources like Google Drive and Slack in any format.
The platform streamlines model management, enabling developers to choose from options like OpenAI or Hugging Face seamlessly.
Integrating AI functionalities into apps is made as simple as writing a single line of code via API or SDKs.
Video clip demonstrating short Javascript semantic search functionality.
Just connect your data, select your AI stack, and start building with just one line of code.
